analysis.one_liner: Requires congressional district maps to be drawn by independent, nonpartisan commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would take congressional map-drawing away from state legislatures, has sat without a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee since it was referred there on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every state to draw its congressional districts using an independent commission with equal numbers of members from the two largest parties and no elected officials on it. It would also cut off federal election-administration money to any state that does not draw its own legislative districts with such a commission. It has been stuck in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where the majority party currently draws district lines to keep itself safe. Balanced, independent commissions mean more competitive districts, so representatives have to win over the whole electorate instead of just their party's primary voters. State-level voters also gain, since the bill ties federal election funds to commission-drawn state legislative maps.

how_it_helps.text: Requires congressional redistricting in every state to follow a plan developed by a commission whose members are split evenly between the two largest parties, with no elected officials allowed on it — taking map-drawing power away from the politicians whose seats the maps protect.

Prohibits states from using federal election-administration funds unless they certify to the Election Assistance Commission that their state legislative districts are also drawn by an independent nonpartisan commission, extending the reform beyond congressional maps.
By removing map-drawing from partisan legislatures, the bill aims to reduce the practice of drawing safe seats, which the bill's title frames as anti-corruption reform for a 'Citizen Legislature'.

analysis.who_pays: State legislatures and party officials lose their power to draw district lines. States that refuse to switch to commission-drawn legislative maps would lose federal money for running elections, so state election offices could bear a budget cost for noncompliance. Incumbent members of Congress in both parties face the loss of safely drawn seats.

drawbacks.text: The requirement applies retroactively, beginning with redistricting carried out after the 2020 census, which would force a wholesale mid-decade redrawing of congressional maps nationwide and disrupt existing districts and representation mid-cycle.

The definition of a 'nonpartisan independent' commission is thin: it only requires an even split between the two largest parties and that members not be elected officials. It does not bar lobbyists, party staff, or insiders from serving, and it says nothing about how commissioners are selected, so a commission could still be captured by political interests.

Conditioning federal election-administration money on states adopting commission-drawn legislative maps is a blunt federal lever on state processes; a state that preferred its own method would have to give up funds meant for running elections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: politicians drawing the maps that decide who can unseat them. If enacted, its effect on electoral competition could be substantial, and the direct cost to taxpayers is small. But the design is rough — a retroactive mid-decade redraw of every state's congressional map, a commission definition that a determined party could game, and a funding cut-off that pressures states through their election budgets. A better-built version would specify commissioner selection and phase in at the next census.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2025 and has received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the CLEAN Elections Act on January 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action recorded in its history so far.
Five Democratic representatives have signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a single Republican sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled, and the bill remains in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: incumbent members of both parties keep districts drawn by the state legislatures and partisan map-makers the bill would displace, and no one has had to defend the current map-drawing system in a hearing or vote.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CLEAN Elections Act on January 3, 2025, requiring independent nonpartisan redistricting commissions.

for.name: Five House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 3, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the House floor; the Speaker's office decides which bills get floor time and none was scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship is lightly bipartisan — one Republican sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors — but with no hearing or vote on record, how the parties would line up is untested.

industries.note: Gerrymandered maps let legislators effectively choose their voters; commission-drawn, partisan-balanced maps would force many to win competitive general elections instead of safe districts. Their interest in keeping the current system runs directly against voters' interest in competitive choice.

industries.industry: State legislatures and state party organizations
industries.note: These bodies currently control congressional and (in most states) legislative map-drawing; the bill strips that power and withholds federal election funds from states that don't switch to commissions.

analysis.trajectory: Redistricting bills like this almost always die in committee, and the odds are worse than usual now: both parties currently benefit from legislature-drawn maps somewhere, and the 2025-26 mid-decade redistricting fights have made map control a top partisan priority. With no hearing after a year and a half, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the Judiciary Committee until this Congress ends.
